title: Semantic versus syntactic multilinear circuits
formal: Is there a field \(F\), fixed independently of \(n\), and a family \(f_n\in F[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), \(n\ge1\), that has polynomial-size semantically multilinear arithmetic circuits over \(F\) but has no polynomial-size family of syntactically multilinear arithmetic circuits over that same field? Semantic multilinearity is required at every gate. The question uses nonuniform circuit size and allows arbitrary field constants.
why: Many arithmetic lower bounds are proved under syntactic restrictions that make the variables entering a multiplication disjoint. Semantic multilinearity permits the same polynomial property to hold after cancellation and sharing of intermediate computations. Determining whether this distinction changes polynomial circuit power would clarify the scope of a central restricted model of algebraic computation.
status_note: The original 2010 survey poses the comparison, and the checked January 2026 primary manuscript still describes semantic multilinearity as potentially more powerful for circuits. No resolution of the stated fixed-field, nonuniform class comparison was identified in bounded searches through 2026-09-15. This does not certify the absence of all later work.

importance.reason: This tests whether the structural multilinearity restriction used in major arithmetic lower-bound models faithfully captures all circuits whose intermediate polynomials are multilinear. A superpolynomial gap would expose a fundamental loss caused by the restriction, while equality would justify its reach beyond formulas.
importance.basis: Individual review of Shpilka–Yehudayoff Open Problem 4 and the 2026 multilinear-complexity discussion; scientific judgment, not a claim of current-status certainty.

sentences: A multilinear polynomial uses each variable with exponent at most one in every nonzero monomial.
Semantic multilinearity requires this property at every arithmetic-circuit gate after cancellation.
Syntactic multilinearity instead requires the variable-occurrence sets entering each multiplication to be disjoint.
The question asks whether one polynomial family over a fixed field can have polynomial semantic circuits but no polynomial syntactic circuits.
Formulas admit size-preserving conversion, while the checked 2026 discussion retains the possibility of greater semantic power for circuits with shared outputs.

definitions: A field is a commutative field with \(0\ne1\); it may be finite or infinite and is chosen once for the entire family. An arithmetic circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output. Input gates are labelled by variables in \(\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\) or by arbitrary elements of \(F\). Every internal gate has two input wires and is labelled \(+\) or \(\times\). Wires may reuse gate outputs, including as the two inputs of a gate, and both wires are then counted. Every gate lies on a path to the output. Size is one plus the number of wires; a field constant occupies one input gate irrespective of any representation length. There is no bound on depth or fan-out, no division gate, and no requirement that a circuit or its constants can be computed from \(n\). Each gate computes its formal polynomial in the polynomial ring \(F[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\). A polynomial is multilinear if every monomial with nonzero coefficient has exponent at most one in each variable; the zero polynomial is multilinear. A circuit is semantically multilinear if every gate computes such a polynomial, after all cancellations in \(F\). For each gate \(g\), let \(\operatorname{Var}(g)\) be the set of variable labels occurring at input gates from which there is a directed path to \(g\), whether or not those variables cancel from its polynomial. A circuit is syntactically multilinear if \(\operatorname{Var}(g_1)\cap\operatorname{Var}(g_2)=\varnothing\) at every product gate with children \(g_1,g_2\). No such disjointness is required at addition gates. Let \(s_{\mathrm{sem},F}(f)\) and \(s_{\mathrm{syn},F}(f)\) be the minimum sizes of the respective circuits computing exactly \(f\). Equality means equality of formal polynomials, including over finite fields. Both minima are finite for a multilinear polynomial. Precisely, the target asks for \(F,(f_n)_{n\ge1},C>0,k\in\mathbb N\) such that \(\forall n\ge1,\ s_{\mathrm{sem},F}(f_n)\le C(n+1)^k\), while \(\forall B>0\;\forall d\in\mathbb N\;\forall N\ge1\;\exists n\ge N,\ s_{\mathrm{syn},F}(f_n)>B(n+1)^d\). Thus superpolynomial separation means failure of every polynomial bound for the family, with violations arbitrarily far out; an eventually exponential lower bound is not required. The field and family are existentially quantified before these asymptotic bounds.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the stated fixed-field family separation, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A positive answer must establish polynomial semantic size and failure of every polynomial syntactic size bound for one family over one fixed field. A negative answer must show that over every field, each polynomial-size semantically multilinear family also has polynomial-size syntactically multilinear circuits, with polynomial constants allowed to depend on that field and family. No effective circuit-conversion algorithm is additionally required. A separation involving unrestricted intermediate polynomials, formulas only, bounded-depth circuits only or Boolean-function equality does not settle this comparison.

context_blocks.text: Open Problem 4 in the 2010 survey compares multilinear circuits with syntactically multilinear circuits. The adjacent Open Problem 3 compares unrestricted circuits with multilinear circuits and is a different question. Semantic multilinearity here follows the gate-by-gate definition used by the survey.

The survey leaves the ground field implicit under its arbitrary-field convention. This card makes the fixed-field interpretation explicit: a separation may occur over some field, but that field must remain the same at every family size. It does not require separation over every field or allow the field to vary with the input length.

Syntactic multilinearity implies semantic multilinearity. The reverse implication for the given circuit need not hold, because a variable may occur in a subcircuit without occurring in its resulting polynomial. The question concerns the minimum sizes of alternative circuits computing the same polynomial.

The survey’s Theorem 2.4, attributed to Raz, states that a multilinear formula can be made syntactically multilinear without increasing its wire count. The open comparison concerns circuits with shared intermediate outputs, where that formula statement does not settle polynomial-size equivalence.

A January 2026 paper by Borém Fabris, Limaye, Srinivasan and Yehudayoff still describes semantic multilinearity as potentially more powerful for circuits and branching programs. Its main results concern syntactic multilinear branching programs and a lower-bound method; they do not claim the semantic-versus-syntactic circuit separation.
